screens.title: SOLID Principles — Single Responsibility & Open/Closed
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will study two foundational SOLID principles that shape maintainable, extensible object-oriented systems. First, we’ll learn the Single Responsibility Principle, which asks you to give a class only one primary reason to change. That keeps classes small, testable, and easier to understand. Second, we’ll explore the Open/Closed Principle, which asks that code be open for extension but closed for modification — so adding new behavior usually means adding new code, not altering existing, tested code. You’ll see concrete examples: a report-generator that mixes data, formatting, and delivery; an order object that also persists and notifies; and a discount calculator that mutates with every new customer type. We’ll refactor these examples by separating responsibilities into focused collaborators and by introducing abstractions and polymorphic implementations. Along the way I’ll point out common mistakes like God objects and over-fragmentation, and give practical advice for when to apply each principle. By the end you’ll know how to identify SRP and OCP violations in code, perform targeted refactors, and choose the right level of abstraction so systems remain robust as requirements change. What do you want to protect from accidental change in your next design?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Overview
SOLID: Single Responsibility & Open/Closed
Build classes that change for only one reason, and modules that gain features without breaking working code.
In this lesson
Identify SRP and OCP violations, perform refactors, and design abstractions using Python examples that keep systems stable as they grow.
Coming up
Hands-on refactor of a Logger, refactor patterns for reports and discounts, and assessment scenarios to test your understanding.
Concept Map

One reason to change: split data, persistence, and delivery.
OCP
Add new behaviors via new types implementing a common contract.
Result
Systems resist accidental regressions when requirements change.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Follow live refactors and code walkthroughs that map to practical maintenance tasks.
Timebox

OCP: Use abstraction
Refactoring patterns
Practical refactors and patterns you can apply immediately to reduce future maintenance cost.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will perform four practical design skills that matter in real-world systems. First, you will define the Single Responsibility Principle clearly and judge whether a class has more than one reason to change. That skill helps you spot brittle code before it breaks. Second, you will identify SRP violations in existing code and refactor them into focused collaborators, improving testability and reducing coupling. Third, you will explain the Open/Closed Principle and recognize when a design forces modification for every new feature rather than allowing safe extension. Fourth, you will apply abstraction and polymorphism to make code open for extension but closed for modification, for example by creating exporter or customer-type classes. Each objective includes an example and a milestone you can use to verify competency: refactor a logger, design a report exporter, and refactor a discount calculator so it no longer requires if/else changes. These are practical, testable skills you can use immediately in maintenance tasks and code reviews.

screens.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
screens.narratorSegment: The Single Responsibility Principle means each class should focus on a single primary responsibility. Practically, that means you identify the distinct axes of change in your domain and avoid combining them in one type. For example, persistence, presentation, and notification are different axes. When they live together, a change in the way you persist data forces changes in unrelated behavior like formatting output or sending notifications. A concise definition: a class should have only one reason to change. To practice, look at a class that queries a database, formats a report, and emails it. That single class now reacts to database schema changes, output format changes, and email delivery changes — three reasons to change. The SRP response is to separate responsibilities into small collaborators: one class fetches data, one formats it, and one delivers it. This reduces coupling and makes unit tests precise. A common misconception is that SRP demands one method per class or that every tiny behavior must be factored out. Avoid over-fragmentation: keep related behaviors together when they truly change together. The rule of thumb is to group code by shared reason to change. Key takeaway: favor cohesion over arbitrary splitting, and let classes represent a single, well-scoped responsibility.

keyIdea.title: SRP in one line
keyIdea.text: Give each class exactly one primary reason to change to improve cohesion and testability.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Single Responsibility
Definition & Importance
A class should have only one reason to change. This improves cohesion and makes unit tests and maintenance simpler.
Why it matters
Limits the blast radius of changes and clarifies where to modify behavior when requirements change.
Misconception
SRP does not mean extreme fragmentation. Keep related responsibilities together if they always change together.
Key takeaway
Find axes of change and separate them into focused classes to reduce coupling.
Concrete example and analogy
Consider a report pipeline. If fetching data, formatting, and sending email are combined, a schema change, format change, or SMTP change all require edits in one file. Split into ReportDataFetcher, ReportFormatter, and ReportSender. Think of each class like a specialist in a small team: one person gathers ingredients, another cooks, another serves.
Example Card
Before: ReportGenerator mixes DB, format, email. After: three focused classes each with one reason to change.
Key Takeaway

Aim for one axis of change per class; group code by the reason that would cause it to change.

screens.title: ReportGenerator: Mixing Responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a typical SRP violation to make the problem concrete. Imagine a ReportGenerator class that queries the database, formats results into PDF or CSV, and sends the report by email. When the database schema changes, you edit the query logic. When a stakeholder requests CSV instead of PDF, you change formatting. When the mail server settings change, you modify email sending. Each change touches the same class, increasing risk. The example in the chapter shows exactly this: data fetching, formatting, and sending combined. Refactoring breaks these responsibilities into three roles: ReportDataFetcher, ReportFormatter, and ReportSender. The generator becomes an orchestrator that composes those collaborators. This approach lets you unit-test each role independently, swap implementations (for example, replace file-based formatting with a streaming exporter), and avoid regressions when one axis changes. A practical misconception is to only move methods without defining clear interfaces; take the time to design small, intention-revealing methods and clear contracts between collaborators. Conclude by asking: which parts of your classes change for unrelated reasons right now, and which collaborators would make that change safer? ReportGenerator: Mixing Responsibilities means combining data access, formatting, and delivery in one class creates multiple reasons to change; split them into focused collaborators.. In practical terms, why fetching data, formatting, and sending together becomes brittle. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › ReportGenerator Violation
Example (conceptual)
class ReportGenerator:
    def generate(self):
        data = self._query_database()
        report = self._format_pdf(data)
        self._send_email(report)
This triple responsibility binds unrelated changes to a single class. Tests must mock multiple concerns and refactors are riskier.
Refactor plan
  1. Extract data access to ReportDataFetcher with a clear API.
  2. Extract formatting to ReportFormatter with export method.
  3. Extract delivery into ReportSender or EmailService.
  4. Make the orchestrator compose those collaborators and delegate.
Key Takeaway

Refactor by responsibility, not by method. Define clear contracts between components.

screens.title: Refactoring into Collaborators
screens.narratorSegment: A practical refactor converts a monolithic class into a small team of collaborators with clear responsibilities. For reporting, create ReportDataFetcher to encapsulate the query and any mapping logic. This class is the only one that changes when the schema evolves. Create ReportFormatter to accept raw data and produce the desired output format. If you need both PDF and CSV later, you can implement separate formatters without changing the fetcher or sender. Finally, create ReportSender or EmailService that knows how to route and deliver generated bytes. The orchestrator, for example ReportGenerator, composes these collaborators and only coordinates them — it does not perform data access, formatting, or delivery itself. Benefits include single-focus unit tests, the ability to mock collaborators in isolation, and reduced coupling. One tradeoff is designing the contracts carefully: thin, intention-revealing interfaces make swapping implementations straightforward. Resist premature abstraction but design interfaces where changes are likely. A useful design question: when a change occurs, which single collaborator should be updated? If the answer is obvious, your responsibilities are well scoped. Refactoring into Collaborators means small, focused collaborators make changes local and tests targeted — composition preserves behavior while improving modularity.. In practical terms, designing reportdatafetcher, reportformatter, and reportsender. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Refactor Architecture
Component Boxes
ReportDataFetcher
Encapsulates queries and mapping. Only changes when the schema or source changes.
ReportFormatter
Accepts data and renders PDF, CSV, or other formats. New formats are new implementations.
ReportSender
Delivers output to email, storage, or stream. Implementations vary by destination.
Orchestration & Contracts
The orchestrator composes fetcher, formatter, and sender. Define small interfaces like fetch(), format(data), send(output) so collaborators are swappable and testable.
Concrete benefit

When a new report format arrives, add a formatter class; when storage changes, update only the sender. The orchestrator stays unchanged.

screens.title: Order Example: From Violation to Clean Design
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter demonstrates the Order class that mixes business calculation, persistence, and email notifications. Initially, Order contains calculate_total, save_to_database, and send_confirmation_email methods. This violates SRP because changes to pricing, storage, or notification each require altering the same class. The correct approach keeps domain logic in Order — for example, items, owner, and calculate_total — and moves persistence to OrderRepository and notifications to EmailService. The orchestrator code then composes these collaborators: create the Order, call repository. save(order), and call email_service. send_confirmation(order). This pattern yields several advantages: the domain model is a focused, testable unit; persistence strategies can change without touching business logic; and notification implementations can be extended to new channels. A common pitfall is to create rigid dependencies by instantiating concrete repositories inside the Order class. Prefer dependency injection or composition so tests can substitute fakes. Consider this question: if your tests need to mock persistence and notifications, why should they be inside the same class? Order Example: From Violation to Clean Design means keep domain calculations in the domain class and move persistence and notification to separate services for clarity and testability.. In practical terms, separate domain logic, persistence, and notifications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Order Refactor
SRP Violation (conceptual)
class Order:
    def calculate_total(self): ...
    def save_to_database(self): ...
    def send_confirmation_email(self): ...
Tests must mock multiple concerns and business logic may be harder to reason about inside a multi-purpose class.
Refactored collaborators
Order
Holds items and business methods like calculate_total only.
OrderRepository
Handles persistence and can be swapped for different storage backends.
EmailService
Handles notification delivery and formats messages based on order data.
Common Mistake

Instantiating concrete services inside domain objects creates tight coupling and makes testing harder. Prefer passing collaborators in.

screens.title: God Objects and Over-Fragmentation
screens.narratorSegment: Two complementary dangers appear when applying SRP: creating God objects that do too much, and over-fragmenting code into many tiny classes that increase indirection. God objects centralize behavior and become difficult to maintain because many unrelated changes funnel through them. They violate SRP and increase coupling. On the other hand, splitting responsibilities into many micro-classes can make reading and debugging harder because behavior is spread across many files and the call graph grows. The right balance comes from grouping code by the reason to change. If a set of methods always change together, keep them together; if they change for separate reasons, split them. Use cohesion and change history as guides: if tests or change requests consistently target the same cluster of methods, they share a change axis. Also prefer intention-revealing names and small, meaningful interfaces rather than mechanical extraction. A practical rule: extract when you can write a focused unit test for the extracted piece and when it simplifies the original class’s responsibilities. Ask: does this extraction reduce the cognitive load of the original class? God Objects and Over-Fragmentation means avoid god objects and avoid needless fragmentation; group code by shared reasons to change and extract when it simplifies responsibility.. In practical terms, finding the right level of decomposition. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Avoid God objects and avoid needless fragmentation; group code by shared reasons to change and extract when it simplifies responsibility.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Tradeoffs
God Object
Signs: one class touches many domains, has many methods, and is the central point for unrelated changes. This creates brittleness and hidden coupling.
Analogy: a manager who performs every specialist role at the company.
Over-fragmentation
Signs: many tiny classes with thin methods, high indirection, and heavy wiring. Debugging requires jumping between many files.
Analogy: splitting a simple paragraph into sentences across many books.
Practical guidance
  • Group by reason to change: use version control and change history as signals.
  • Extract when tests and responsibilities become clearer, not for its own sake.
  • Prefer clear interfaces that reveal intent, making collaborators easy to swap.

Fourth, apply OCP by creating a ConsoleWriter or DatabaseWriter later; adding these requires only new classes, not changes to Logger. While refactoring, keep tests green by introducing small, incremental changes and using dependency injection to pass collaborators. A common pitfall is copying formatting logic into multiple places; instead centralize formatting in the formatter class so all writers use the same format. After the activity, verify that adding a ConsoleWriter required zero changes to Logger and that you can unit-test the formatter and writers independently. Starter code (concept)
class Logger:
    def _format_message(self, level, message): ...
    def log_info(self, message): ...
    def _write_to_file(self, message): ...

  2. Define LogWriter interface with write(formatted_message).
  3. Implement FileWriter and ConsoleWriter subclasses of LogWriter.

screens.title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
screens.narratorSegment: The Open/Closed Principle states that software entities should be open to extension but closed to direct modification. In practice, this means you design a system so new behavior can be introduced by adding new code — new classes or modules — rather than changing existing, proven code. The primary tools for OCP are abstraction and polymorphism: define a contract or abstract base, then implement concrete behaviors that adhere to that contract. For example, if a DiscountCalculator computes discounts based on customer type, instead of adding conditional branches for each new type, let customer objects provide a discount rate through a method. The calculator then remains unchanged as new customer types are added. A common mistake is overusing abstractions for every change; apply OCP where changes are likely and expensive to modify. Balance is important: use interfaces where extension paths are predictable and implementational details should vary. The core benefit is stability: tested modules remain unchanged while the system grows through new, well-scoped types. Think about where requirements change most often and protect those boundaries with abstractions. Open/Closed Principle (OCP) means protect stable code by adding new types for new behavior rather than editing existing implementations.. In practical terms, open for extension, closed for modification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition & Mechanism
Open for extension, closed for modification. Use abstract interfaces and polymorphism as mechanisms to extend behavior without changing existing code.
When to apply
Apply OCP where features evolve frequently or where making changes has high risk. Avoid premature abstraction for rare changes.
Concrete contrast

screens.title: DiscountCalculator Anti-pattern
screens.narratorSegment: A common OCP violation appears when business logic branches on type codes or strings. Consider a DiscountCalculator that checks customer. type and applies hardcoded rates in an if/elif chain. Each time you introduce a new customer category, you change the calculator. That spreads changes across a core, tested function and increases the chance of regression. The chapter shows this exact pattern: adding VIP required editing calculate_discount. The better solution is to give each customer type an implementation that returns a discount rate. Using an abstract base for Customer with a get_discount_rate method, you create StandardCustomer, PremiumCustomer, and VIPCustomer. DiscountCalculator then multiplies amount by customer. get_discount_rate without requiring changes. This makes adding WholesaleCustomer a matter of adding a new class. A practical pitfall is copying the rate logic across many places; centralize it in each customer class and prefer composition for complex discount strategies. Ask yourself: when a new variant appears, does adding it require touching multiple existing modules? If yes, you likely have an OCP violation. DiscountCalculator Anti-pattern means if new variants force edits to core logic, replace conditionals with polymorphic implementations that the core delegates to.. In practical terms, why conditionals for each type are brittle. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › DiscountCalculator
OCP Violation (concept)
def calculate_discount(customer, amount):
    if customer.type == 'Standard':
        return amount * 0.05
    elif customer.type == 'Premium':
        return amount * 0.10
    elif customer.type == 'VIP':
        return amount * 0.15
Each new type forces edits to this function, which is brittle and violates OCP.
Polymorphic alternative
Define a Customer interface with get_discount_rate, then implement concrete customers. The calculator simply calls customer.get_discount_rate and multiplies the amount.
Key Takeaway

Replace type-checked conditionals with a polymorphic contract to keep calculation code stable as types evolve.

screens.title: Abstraction & Polymorphism: Customer Example
screens.narratorSegment: To apply OCP, introduce a small abstraction that captures the variation point. In the discount example, define an abstract Customer base with a get_discount_rate method. This shifts responsibility for rates to customer types and keeps the calculator closed to modification. You gain the ability to add new behaviors by adding new classes only. screens.title: ReportExporter Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: A practical OCP application from the chapter is the ReportExporter pattern. Define an abstract ReportExporter with a single export(data) method. Implement PdfReportExporter and CsvReportExporter that adhere to this contract. ReportGenerator accepts a ReportExporter instance and delegates export responsibilities to it. Adding Excel or JSON exporters becomes a matter of creating a new exporter class. This preserves the generator’s behavior and reduces risk when adding formats. The pattern also pairs well with SRP: the generator orchestrates but does not know about formatting details, and exporters focus purely on output format. Avoid making exporters too heavy: keep them responsible for producing output from given data and not for fetching or delivering. If delivery is needed, separate it into a sender. This separation keeps code composable, testable, and easy to evolve. When designing the exporter interface, prefer minimal methods so implementations remain simple to test and reason about. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › ReportExporter
Pattern overview
The exporter interface isolates format-specific logic. The generator provides data and relies on exporter.export to produce output.
Benefits
New formats require new exporter classes; the generator code remains unchanged and safe.
Conceptual snippet
class ReportExporter:  # abstract
    def export(self, data): pass

class PdfReportExporter(ReportExporter):
    def export(self, data): ...

class ReportGenerator:
    def __init__(self, exporter):
        self.exporter = exporter
    def generate(self, data):
        return self.exporter.export(data)
This composition satisfies OCP and keeps responsibilities separated.

screens.title: Combining SRP and OCP Effectively
screens.narratorSegment: Good system design combines SRP and OCP: use SRP to keep components focused and use OCP to make those components extensible. In practice, start by identifying responsibilities and extracting focused collaborators. Then ask which collaborators will need variation over time. Those become the candidates for small abstractions. The orchestrator composes collaborators and coordinates flow while remaining stable. Use dependency injection so you can swap implementations in tests and at runtime. Avoid two mistakes: first, over-abstracting everything, which increases indirection; second, under-abstracting variation points, which forces modification later. A pragmatic approach: extract a collaborator if it simplifies the original class and write at least one focused unit test for it. Next, introduce an interface around the collaborator if you expect different implementations. For example, separate a formatter and then make it an exporter interface only if you expect multiple formats. This staged approach reduces upfront complexity and preserves flexibility. Finally, ask yourself: does this change reduce the number of modules you must edit when requirements change? If so, it's a good refactor. Combining SRP and OCP Effectively means extract responsibilities first, then introduce interfaces at likely variation points to make systems easier to evolve.. In practical terms, orchestration, interfaces, and pragmatic trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

  1. Identify responsibilities and extract focused collaborators.
  2. Write tests for the extracted collaborator to validate behavior.
  3. Introduce an interface if multiple implementations are likely.

Tradeoffs & checklist

  • Can collaborators be tested independently?
  • Is the abstraction minimal and intention-revealing?

Use SRP to create focused components and OCP to protect variation points — evolve your design in small, testable steps.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the core ideas you should carry forward. First, the Single Responsibility Principle: a class should have only one reason to change. That leads to more cohesive, testable, and understandable code. Second, the Open/Closed Principle: design modules so new behavior is added by new types rather than by changing existing, tested code. Use abstraction and polymorphism to achieve this. Third, avoid God objects that accumulate too many responsibilities; they become fragile maintenance hotspots. Fourth, apply abstraction pragmatically — protect likely variation points, but avoid premature generalization. Finally, practice the refactor pattern: extract a focused collaborator, write a test for it, and if you expect variants, introduce a small interface. These habits help you keep systems resilient as they grow. Now reflect: what single class in your current codebase would benefit most from a focused refactor?

Single Reason?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will study two foundational SOLID principles that shape maintainable, extensible object-oriented systems. First, we’ll learn the Single Responsibility Principle, which asks you to give a class only one primary reason to change. That keeps classes small, testable, and easier to understand. Second, we’ll explore the Open/Closed Principle, which asks that code be open for extension but closed for modification — so adding new behavior usually means adding new code, not altering existing, tested code. You’ll see concrete examples: a report-generator that mixes data, formatting, and delivery; an order object that also persists and notifies; and a discount calculator that mutates with every new customer type. We’ll refactor these examples by separating responsibilities into focused collaborators and by introducing abstractions and polymorphic implementations. Along the way I’ll point out common mistakes like God objects and over-fragmentation, and give practical advice for when to apply each principle. By the end you’ll know how to identify SRP and OCP violations in code, perform targeted refactors, and choose the right level of abstraction so systems remain robust as requirements change. What do you want to protect from accidental change in your next design?

By the end of this chapter you will perform four practical design skills that matter in real-world systems. First, you will define the Single Responsibility Principle clearly and judge whether a class has more than one reason to change. That skill helps you spot brittle code before it breaks. Second, you will identify SRP violations in existing code and refactor them into focused collaborators, improving testability and reducing coupling. Third, you will explain the Open/Closed Principle and recognize when a design forces modification for every new feature rather than allowing safe extension. Fourth, you will apply abstraction and polymorphism to make code open for extension but closed for modification, for example by creating exporter or customer-type classes. Each objective includes an example and a milestone you can use to verify competency: refactor a logger, design a report exporter, and refactor a discount calculator so it no longer requires if/else changes. These are practical, testable skills you can use immediately in maintenance tasks and code reviews.

This second objectives page focuses on practical outcomes and an assessment mindset. You will complete a refactor of a logging system that currently formats messages and writes them to a file. First, identify the two responsibilities and separate them into a formatter and a writer. Second, design the writer so you can swap destinations without changing the logger itself, for example adding a console or database destination later. Third, refactor the report generation example into exporter implementations so new formats require new exporter classes, not changes to the report generator. Finally, practice spotting OCP violations such as adding new conditional branches for each variant. These tasks are small but powerful: they teach you to protect tested behavior, to make safe change, and to keep future additions local to new modules. Use the provided starter code to practice, and verify competence by showing that adding a new destination or exporter required zero changes to the orchestrator class.

The Single Responsibility Principle means each class should focus on a single primary responsibility. Practically, that means you identify the distinct axes of change in your domain and avoid combining them in one type. For example, persistence, presentation, and notification are different axes. When they live together, a change in the way you persist data forces changes in unrelated behavior like formatting output or sending notifications. A concise definition: a class should have only one reason to change. To practice, look at a class that queries a database, formats a report, and emails it. That single class now reacts to database schema changes, output format changes, and email delivery changes — three reasons to change. The SRP response is to separate responsibilities into small collaborators: one class fetches data, one formats it, and one delivers it. This reduces coupling and makes unit tests precise. A common misconception is that SRP demands one method per class or that every tiny behavior must be factored out. Avoid over-fragmentation: keep related behaviors together when they truly change together. The rule of thumb is to group code by shared reason to change. Key takeaway: favor cohesion over arbitrary splitting, and let classes represent a single, well-scoped responsibility.

Let's walk through a typical SRP violation to make the problem concrete. Imagine a ReportGenerator class that queries the database, formats results into PDF or CSV, and sends the report by email. When the database schema changes, you edit the query logic. When a stakeholder requests CSV instead of PDF, you change formatting. When the mail server settings change, you modify email sending. Each change touches the same class, increasing risk. The example in the chapter shows exactly this: data fetching, formatting, and sending combined. Refactoring breaks these responsibilities into three roles: ReportDataFetcher, ReportFormatter, and ReportSender. The generator becomes an orchestrator that composes those collaborators. This approach lets you unit-test each role independently, swap implementations (for example, replace file-based formatting with a streaming exporter), and avoid regressions when one axis changes. A practical misconception is to only move methods without defining clear interfaces; take the time to design small, intention-revealing methods and clear contracts between collaborators. Conclude by asking: which parts of your classes change for unrelated reasons right now, and which collaborators would make that change safer? ReportGenerator: Mixing Responsibilities means combining data access, formatting, and delivery in one class creates multiple reasons to change; split them into focused collaborators.. In practical terms, why fetching data, formatting, and sending together becomes brittle. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A practical refactor converts a monolithic class into a small team of collaborators with clear responsibilities. For reporting, create ReportDataFetcher to encapsulate the query and any mapping logic. This class is the only one that changes when the schema evolves. Create ReportFormatter to accept raw data and produce the desired output format. If you need both PDF and CSV later, you can implement separate formatters without changing the fetcher or sender. Finally, create ReportSender or EmailService that knows how to route and deliver generated bytes. The orchestrator, for example ReportGenerator, composes these collaborators and only coordinates them — it does not perform data access, formatting, or delivery itself. Benefits include single-focus unit tests, the ability to mock collaborators in isolation, and reduced coupling. One tradeoff is designing the contracts carefully: thin, intention-revealing interfaces make swapping implementations straightforward. Resist premature abstraction but design interfaces where changes are likely. A useful design question: when a change occurs, which single collaborator should be updated? If the answer is obvious, your responsibilities are well scoped. Refactoring into Collaborators means small, focused collaborators make changes local and tests targeted — composition preserves behavior while improving modularity.. In practical terms, designing reportdatafetcher, reportformatter, and reportsender. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The chapter demonstrates the Order class that mixes business calculation, persistence, and email notifications. Initially, Order contains calculate_total, save_to_database, and send_confirmation_email methods. This violates SRP because changes to pricing, storage, or notification each require altering the same class. The correct approach keeps domain logic in Order — for example, items, owner, and calculate_total — and moves persistence to OrderRepository and notifications to EmailService. The orchestrator code then composes these collaborators: create the Order, call repository. save(order), and call email_service. send_confirmation(order). This pattern yields several advantages: the domain model is a focused, testable unit; persistence strategies can change without touching business logic; and notification implementations can be extended to new channels. A common pitfall is to create rigid dependencies by instantiating concrete repositories inside the Order class. Prefer dependency injection or composition so tests can substitute fakes. Consider this question: if your tests need to mock persistence and notifications, why should they be inside the same class? Order Example: From Violation to Clean Design means keep domain calculations in the domain class and move persistence and notification to separate services for clarity and testability.. In practical terms, separate domain logic, persistence, and notifications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Two complementary dangers appear when applying SRP: creating God objects that do too much, and over-fragmenting code into many tiny classes that increase indirection. God objects centralize behavior and become difficult to maintain because many unrelated changes funnel through them. They violate SRP and increase coupling. On the other hand, splitting responsibilities into many micro-classes can make reading and debugging harder because behavior is spread across many files and the call graph grows. The right balance comes from grouping code by the reason to change. If a set of methods always change together, keep them together; if they change for separate reasons, split them. Use cohesion and change history as guides: if tests or change requests consistently target the same cluster of methods, they share a change axis. Also prefer intention-revealing names and small, meaningful interfaces rather than mechanical extraction. A practical rule: extract when you can write a focused unit test for the extracted piece and when it simplifies the original class’s responsibilities. Ask: does this extraction reduce the cognitive load of the original class? The Open/Closed Principle states that software entities should be open to extension but closed to direct modification. In practice, this means you design a system so new behavior can be introduced by adding new code — new classes or modules — rather than changing existing, proven code. The primary tools for OCP are abstraction and polymorphism: define a contract or abstract base, then implement concrete behaviors that adhere to that contract. For example, if a DiscountCalculator computes discounts based on customer type, instead of adding conditional branches for each new type, let customer objects provide a discount rate through a method. The calculator then remains unchanged as new customer types are added. A common mistake is overusing abstractions for every change; apply OCP where changes are likely and expensive to modify. Balance is important: use interfaces where extension paths are predictable and implementational details should vary. The core benefit is stability: tested modules remain unchanged while the system grows through new, well-scoped types. Think about where requirements change most often and protect those boundaries with abstractions. A common OCP violation appears when business logic branches on type codes or strings. Consider a DiscountCalculator that checks customer. type and applies hardcoded rates in an if/elif chain. Each time you introduce a new customer category, you change the calculator. That spreads changes across a core, tested function and increases the chance of regression. The chapter shows this exact pattern: adding VIP required editing calculate_discount. The better solution is to give each customer type an implementation that returns a discount rate. Using an abstract base for Customer with a get_discount_rate method, you create StandardCustomer, PremiumCustomer, and VIPCustomer. DiscountCalculator then multiplies amount by customer. get_discount_rate without requiring changes. This makes adding WholesaleCustomer a matter of adding a new class. Good system design combines SRP and OCP: use SRP to keep components focused and use OCP to make those components extensible. In practice, start by identifying responsibilities and extracting focused collaborators. Then ask which collaborators will need variation over time. Those become the candidates for small abstractions. The orchestrator composes collaborators and coordinates flow while remaining stable. Use dependency injection so you can swap implementations in tests and at runtime. Avoid two mistakes: first, over-abstracting everything, which increases indirection; second, under-abstracting variation points, which forces modification later. A pragmatic approach: extract a collaborator if it simplifies the original class and write at least one focused unit test for it. Next, introduce an interface around the collaborator if you expect different implementations. For example, separate a formatter and then make it an exporter interface only if you expect multiple formats. This staged approach reduces upfront complexity and preserves flexibility. Finally, ask yourself: does this change reduce the number of modules you must edit when requirements change? If so, it's a good refactor. Let's summarize the core ideas you should carry forward. First, the Single Responsibility Principle: a class should have only one reason to change. That leads to more cohesive, testable, and understandable code. Second, the Open/Closed Principle: design modules so new behavior is added by new types rather than by changing existing, tested code. Use abstraction and polymorphism to achieve this. Third, avoid God objects that accumulate too many responsibilities; they become fragile maintenance hotspots. Fourth, apply abstraction pragmatically — protect likely variation points, but avoid premature generalization. Finally, practice the refactor pattern: extract a focused collaborator, write a test for it, and if you expect variants, introduce a small interface. These habits help you keep systems resilient as they grow. Now reflect: what single class in your current codebase would benefit most from a focused refactor?

Before you finish a refactor or review a pull request, run a quick checklist: does each class have one clear reason to change? Are variation points behind interfaces or abstract bases so new behavior can be added without editing core code? Have you avoided creating God objects by splitting responsibilities sensibly? Did you introduce abstractions only where you expect change or multiple implementations? Finally, ensure tests exercise collaborators in isolation and that the orchestrator coordinates rather than implements. These checks help you apply SRP and OCP pragmatically and keep the codebase agile and safe to change.
